title: UNIT 2: CHEMICAL BONDING
notes:
✓ Chemical bonding → Explains how atoms combine to form molecules and compounds.

Atoms form bonds because the resulting arrangement is generally more stable than the separate atoms.

◆ MAIN TYPES OF CHEMICAL BONDING
✓ Ionic bonding.
✓ Covalent bonding.
✓ Metallic bonding.

→ Bonding theories help explain how electrons are involved in bond formation and how molecules obtain their structures and properties.

title: 2.1 Introduction to Chemical Bonding
notes:
✓ Chemical bonds → Attractive forces that hold atoms or ions together in compounds.

✓ Valence electrons → Electrons mainly involved in bonding.

→ Atoms can achieve greater stability by losing, gaining, or sharing electrons.

◆ MAIN TYPES
✓ Ionic bonding.
✓ Covalent bonding.
✓ Metallic bonding.

→ The properties of a substance depend strongly on the type of bonding and the arrangement of its particles.

title: 2.1.1 The Octet Rule
notes:
✓ Octet rule → Atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons so that they achieve a stable arrangement of eight electrons in their valence shell, similar to the electron configuration of a noble gas.

→ Metals commonly achieve stability by losing electrons, while many nonmetals achieve stability by gaining or sharing electrons.

✓ Hydrogen and helium → Exceptions because their first energy level can contain a maximum of two electrons.

→ The octet rule is useful for predicting many bonding arrangements, although some compounds do not follow it exactly.

title: 2.1.2 Types of Chemical Bonding
notes:
◆ THREE MAJOR TYPES

✓ IONIC BONDING → Formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually after electrons are transferred from one atom to another.

✓ COVALENT BONDING → Formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

✓ METALLIC BONDING → Occurs in metals, where positive metal ions are held together by attraction to delocalized electrons.

→ The difference in how valence electrons behave produces different structures and properties.

title: 2.2 Ionic Bonds
notes:
✓ Ionic bond → Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

→ Ionic compounds usually form when a metal transfers one or more electrons to a nonmetal.

✓ Metal → Forms a positive ion (cation).
✓ Nonmetal → Forms a negative ion (anion).

◆ EXAMPLE
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl

→ Ionic bonding involves electron transfer rather than electron sharing.

title: 2.2.1 Lewis Electron-Dot Symbols
notes:
✓ Lewis electron-dot symbols → Represent the valence electrons of an atom using dots around the element symbol.

✓ Sodium → Has one valence electron and can be represented as Na with one dot.
✓ Chlorine → Has seven valence electrons.

→ Lewis symbols are useful for predicting how atoms may gain, lose, or share electrons during chemical bonding.

→ For main-group elements, the number of valence electrons can often be related to the group of the element in the periodic table.

title: 2.2.2 Formation of Ionic Bonds
notes:
✓ Ionic bonds → Form through electron transfer followed by electrostatic attraction between the resulting ions.

◆ MAGNESIUM CHLORIDE
Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
2Cl + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → MgCl₂

✓ Ionic compound → Must be electrically neutral.
→ Total positive charge = Total negative charge.

→ Ionic compounds contain ions arranged in an extended crystal lattice rather than separate molecules.

title: 2.2.3 Exceptions to the Octet Rule in Ionic Compounds
notes:
✓ The octet rule is useful but not universal.

→ Some atoms and compounds can have electron arrangements that do not contain exactly eight electrons around the central atom.

◆ POSSIBLE EXCEPTIONS
✓ Incomplete octets.
✓ Expanded valence shells.

→ The octet rule should therefore be treated as a useful guideline rather than an absolute rule.

✓ Electron configuration, atomic size, and the elements involved → Help determine the actual structure.

title: 2.2.4 Properties of Ionic Compounds
notes:
✓ Ionic compounds → Generally have strong electrostatic attractions between their ions.

◆ IMPORTANT PROPERTIES
✓ Usually high melting and boiling points.
✓ Generally hard and crystalline solids.
✓ Brittle because shifting the lattice can bring like charges close together.
✓ Many are soluble in polar solvents such as water.
✓ Do not normally conduct electricity as solids because their ions are fixed in place.
✓ Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved because the ions can move.

→ These properties result from the strong ionic lattice and the mobility of ions in molten or aqueous states.

title: 2.3 Covalent Bonds and Molecular Geometry
notes:
✓ Covalent bond → Forms when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

→ Covalent bonding commonly occurs between nonmetal atoms.

◆ TYPES OF COVALENT BONDS
✓ Single bond → One shared electron pair.
✓ Double bond → Two shared electron pairs.
✓ Triple bond → Three shared electron pairs.

◆ EXAMPLES
H₂ → H–H
O₂ → O=O
N₂ → N≡N

→ Covalent compounds can exist as individual molecules or as giant covalent structures. Their properties depend strongly on the types of bonds and the arrangement of atoms.

title: 2.3.1 Molecular Geometry
notes:
✓ Molecular geometry → The three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule.

→ The shape of a molecule is strongly influenced by electron pairs around the central atom.

✓ Electron pairs repel one another and tend to arrange themselves as far apart as possible.
→ Both bonding pairs and lone pairs influence molecular shape.

◆ COMMON MOLECULAR GEOMETRIES
✓ Linear → 180°.
✓ Trigonal planar → Approximately 120°.
✓ Tetrahedral → Approximately 109.5°.
✓ Trigonal pyramidal → Approximately 107°.
✓ Bent → Bond angle depends on the number of lone pairs.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ CH₄ → Tetrahedral.
✓ NH₃ → Trigonal pyramidal.
✓ H₂O → Bent.

title: 2.3.2 Intermolecular Forces in Covalent Compounds
notes:
✓ Intermolecular forces → Attractions between molecules.

→ They are generally weaker than the covalent bonds within molecules but strongly influence physical properties such as boiling point, melting point, viscosity, and solubility.

◆ DIPOLE–DIPOLE FORCES
✓ Attractions between polar molecules with permanent partial charges.

◆ HYDROGEN BONDING
✓ A particularly strong intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen bonded to highly electronegative atoms such as nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.

◆ LONDON DISPERSION FORCES
✓ Attractions caused by temporary fluctuations in electron distribution.
✓ Occur in all atoms and molecules.

→ Stronger intermolecular forces generally require more energy to separate molecules.

title: 2.4 Metallic Bonding
notes:
✓ Metallic bonding → Attraction between positively charged metal ions and a sea of delocalized valence electrons.

→ Metal atoms contribute their outer electrons to a shared system in which the electrons are not associated with only one particular atom.

◆ PROPERTIES EXPLAINED BY METALLIC BONDING
✓ Electrical conductivity.
✓ Thermal conductivity.
✓ Malleability.
✓ Ductility.
✓ Metallic luster.

title: 2.4.1 Formation of Metallic Bonding
notes:
✓ Metallic bonding → Occurs when metal atoms release or contribute their valence electrons to a delocalized electron system.

→ Metal atoms become positive centers surrounded by mobile electrons.

✓ Electrostatic attraction → Holds the positive metal centers and delocalized electrons together.

→ Because the electrons are mobile throughout the structure, metals can conduct electricity and heat effectively.

title: 2.4.2 Electron-Sea Model
notes:
✓ Electron-sea model → Describes a metal as a lattice of positive metal ions immersed in a sea of delocalized electrons.

→ The electrons can move through the entire metallic structure rather than being restricted to individual atoms.

◆ METALLIC PROPERTIES EXPLAINED
✓ Conduct electricity.
✓ Conduct heat.
✓ Can be shaped without easily breaking.
✓ Have metallic luster.

→ Mobile electrons are especially important in explaining electrical and thermal conductivity.

title: 2.4.3 Properties of Metals and Metallic Bonding
notes:
✓ Metallic bonding → Gives metals several characteristic properties.

◆ IMPORTANT PROPERTIES
✓ Electrical conductivity → Mobile electrons carry charge.
✓ Thermal conductivity → Electrons help transfer thermal energy.
✓ Malleability → Metals can be hammered into sheets.
✓ Ductility → Metals can be drawn into wires.
✓ Metallic luster → Metals reflect light effectively.
✓ Generally high melting and boiling points → Strong metallic attractions require considerable energy to overcome.

→ The strength of metallic bonding depends on factors such as the number of delocalized electrons and the size and charge of the metal ions.

title: 2.5 Chemical Bonding Theories
notes:
✓ Chemical bonding theories → Provide models for explaining how atoms form bonds and how electrons are distributed in molecules.

◆ TWO IMPORTANT THEORIES
✓ Valence Bond (VB) Theory.
✓ Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT).

✓ Valence Bond Theory → Describes bonding in terms of overlap of atomic orbitals and localized electron pairs.
✓ Molecular Orbital Theory → Treats electrons as occupying molecular orbitals that extend over the molecule.

title: 2.5.1 Valence Bond (VB) Theory
notes:
✓ Valence Bond Theory → Explains covalent bonding as the overlap of atomic orbitals containing electrons with opposite spins.

→ When two atomic orbitals overlap, the electrons can become paired and a covalent bond is formed.
→ Greater effective orbital overlap generally produces a stronger bond.

✓ Hybridization → Used by VB theory to explain molecular geometry.

◆ COMMON HYBRIDIZATIONS
✓ sp → Linear geometry.
✓ sp² → Trigonal planar geometry.
✓ sp³ → Tetrahedral arrangement.

✓ Example: Carbon in CH₄ → Commonly described as sp³ hybridized, giving a tetrahedral molecular geometry.

title: 2.5.2 Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)
notes:
✓ Molecular Orbital Theory → Describes electrons as occupying molecular orbitals formed from combinations of atomic orbitals.

→ Molecular orbitals extend over the entire molecule rather than being restricted to one bond between two atoms.

◆ TYPES OF MOLECULAR ORBITALS
✓ Bonding molecular orbitals → Have lower energy than the original atomic orbitals and help stabilize the molecule.
✓ Antibonding molecular orbitals → Have higher energy and oppose bonding.

→ Electrons fill molecular orbitals according to energy, the Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund’s rule.

✓ MOT → Especially useful for explaining magnetic behavior and molecules that cannot be adequately described using simple localized-bond models.

title: 2.6 Types of Crystal
notes:
✓ Crystal → A solid in which particles are arranged in an orderly, repeating pattern.

→ The particles may be atoms, ions, or molecules.

◆ MAJOR TYPES OF CRYSTALS
✓ Ionic crystals.
✓ Molecular crystals.
✓ Covalent-network crystals.
✓ Metallic crystals.

◆ IONIC CRYSTALS
✓ Positive and negative ions are arranged in a regular lattice and held together by electrostatic attraction.
→ Generally hard, brittle, and have high melting points.

◆ MOLECULAR CRYSTALS
✓ Molecules are held together by intermolecular forces.
→ Generally have lower melting points than ionic or network crystals.

◆ COVALENT-NETWORK CRYSTALS
✓ Atoms are connected by strong covalent bonds throughout an extended network.
✓ Examples → Diamond and silicon dioxide.

◆ METALLIC CRYSTALS
✓ Metal atoms form a lattice held together by metallic bonding and delocalized electrons.
→ Generally conduct heat and electricity well.

title: UNIT 2 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ OCTET RULE → Atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve a stable valence-shell arrangement, commonly eight electrons.

✓ IONIC BOND → Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
✓ COVALENT BOND → Bond formed by sharing electron pairs.
✓ METALLIC BOND → Attraction between positive metal centers and delocalized electrons.

✓ LEWIS SYMBOL → Shows the valence electrons of an atom.

✓ IONIC COMPOUNDS → Usually hard, brittle, high-melting solids; conduct electricity when molten or dissolved.

✓ MOLECULAR GEOMETRY → Three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule.

✓ INTERMOLECULAR FORCES → Attractions between molecules, including London dispersion, dipole–dipole, and hydrogen bonding.

✓ ELECTRON-SEA MODEL → Positive metal ions surrounded by mobile, delocalized electrons.

✓ VB THEORY → Covalent bonds form through overlap of atomic orbitals.
✓ MOT → Electrons occupy molecular orbitals extending over the molecule.

◆ HYBRIDIZATION
✓ sp → Linear.
✓ sp² → Trigonal planar.
✓ sp³ → Tetrahedral.

✓ CRYSTAL TYPES → Ionic, molecular, covalent-network, and metallic crystals.

→ KEY IDEA → The type of chemical bonding determines the structure and many of the physical properties of a substance.
